reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID (Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease)
clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive deficiency of 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase (MCCC1 or MCCC2 genes), a biotin-dependent enzyme in leucine catabolism, and one of the most common organic acidurias detected by newborn screening
Most identified individuals are asymptomatic, so a positive screen frequently represents a benign biochemical phenotype rather than clinical disease
When symptomatic, presentation ranges from metabolic decompensation with hypoglycaemia and metabolic acidosis during catabolic stress to feeding difficulties, hypotonia and developmental delay
Newborn screening flags an elevated C5-OH (3-hydroxyisovalerylcarnitine), which overlaps with several other conditions and must be interpreted with confirmatory testing
Urine organic acids show 3-methylcrotonylglycine and 3-hydroxyisovaleric acid; secondary carnitine depletion is common
Maternal 3-MCC can be detected through an abnormal newborn screen in an unaffected infant, so an asymptomatic mother should be considered

Management, where indicated, includes avoidance of fasting and prolonged catabolism, carnitine supplementation for secondary deficiency, and an emergency regimen with glucose during illness; a biotin trial may be considered although the enzyme defect is not biotin-responsive
reference.pathophysiology: 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase is a biotin-dependent mitochondrial enzyme that catalyses a step in the catabolism of the branched-chain amino acid leucine, converting 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA to 3-methylglutaconyl-CoA. Deficiency blocks leucine breakdown, causing accumulation of 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA derivatives that are excreted as 3-methylcrotonylglycine and 3-hydroxyisovaleric acid and detected as raised 3-hydroxyisovalerylcarnitine (C5-OH). The accumulating metabolites can sequester coenzyme A and carnitine, producing secondary carnitine deficiency. The biochemical defect is frequently clinically silent, but under catabolic stress a minority develop metabolic decompensation, and unlike multiple carboxylase deficiency the isolated enzyme defect is not corrected by biotin.
additionalDifferentials: Multiple carboxylase deficiency (holocarboxylase synthetase or biotinidase deficiency)
Other organic acidaemias raising C5-OH on screening
Maternal 3-MCC detected through the infant's newborn screen
additionalInvestigations: Plasma acylcarnitine profile confirming elevated C5-OH (3-hydroxyisovalerylcarnitine)
Urine organic acids for 3-methylcrotonylglycine and 3-hydroxyisovaleric acid
Plasma free and total carnitine to detect secondary deficiency
Blood glucose, blood gas and ammonia during any symptomatic episode
MCCC1 and MCCC2 molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis
Maternal biochemical testing when an unaffected infant screens positive
redFlags: Metabolic decompensation with hypoglycaemia and acidosis during intercurrent illness
Encephalopathy or reduced consciousness during a catabolic crisis
Failure to thrive, marked hypotonia or developmental regression in a symptomatic child
reference.prognosis: The large majority of individuals identified by newborn screening remain asymptomatic with a normal outlook, but a minority experience metabolic crises and, rarely, neurological sequelae, so counselling should reflect this generally benign but occasionally clinically significant course.
pitfalls: Over-treating or over-investigating an asymptomatic screen-positive child as though clinical disease is certain
Failing to consider maternal 3-MCC when an unaffected infant screens positive
Assuming the enzyme defect is biotin-responsive like multiple carboxylase deficiency
Missing secondary carnitine deficiency during monitoring
references: Scriver's OMMBID: Disorders of Leucine Metabolism
Saudubray, Baumgartner & Walter, Inborn Metabolic Diseases: Diagnosis and Treatment
management: Preventive focus on avoiding catabolism through regular feeding and prompt carbohydrate intake, since the biochemical defect is frequently clinically silent.
Emergency sick-day regimen with high-energy glucose-based feeds or intravenous dextrose during intercurrent illness or fasting.
Carnitine supplementation for the commonly associated secondary carnitine depletion.
Recognition that this isolated enzyme defect is not corrected by biotin, unlike multiple carboxylase deficiency, so biotin is not used as specific therapy.
Prompt correction of hypoglycaemia and metabolic acidosis during any decompensation.
Monitoring of feeding, tone, growth and development, with acylcarnitine and carnitine follow-up.
Genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance and maternal biochemical testing when an unaffected infant screens positive.
